The Master said: The gentleman is not a vessel.

Zigong asked about the gentleman. The Master said: He first acts on his words, and then speaks of them.

宰我问：三年之丧，期已久矣。君子三年不为礼，礼必坏；三年不为乐，乐必崩。旧谷既没，新谷既升，钻燧改火，期可已矣。子曰：食夫稻，衣夫锦，于女安乎？曰：安。女安则为之！夫君子之居丧，食旨不甘，闻乐不乐，居处不安，故不为也。今女安，则为之！宰我出。子曰：予之不仁也！子生三年，然后免于父母之怀。夫三年之丧，天下之通丧也。予也有三年之爱于其父母乎？
Eating one's fill all day
The Master said: To eat one's fill all day and give one's mind to nothing — that is hard indeed! Are there not games like bo and yi? Playing them would still be better than nothing.
/en/lunyu/yang-huo/22.html
子曰：饱食终日，无所用心，难矣哉！不有博弈者乎，为之犹贤乎已。
Does the gentleman esteem courage?

Zilu said: Does the gentleman esteem courage? The Master said: The gentleman holds what is right as highest. Those above who have courage but not rightness make trouble; those below who have courage but not rightness become robbers.
/en/lunyu/yang-huo/23.html
子路曰：君子尚勇乎？子曰：君子义以为上。君子有勇而无义为乱，小人有勇而无义为盗。
Does the gentleman also hate?

Zigong said: Does the gentleman also have things he hates? The Master said: He does. He hates those who speak of others' faults; he hates those in low places who slander those above; he hates the brave who lack ritual; he hates the bold who…
/en/lunyu/yang-huo/24.html
子贡曰：君子亦有恶乎？子曰：有恶：恶称人之恶者，恶居下流而讪上者，恶勇而无礼者，恶果敢而窒者。曰：赐也亦有恶乎？恶徼以为知者，恶不孙以为勇者，恶讦以为直者。
The hardest to deal with
The Master said: Women and servants are the hardest to deal with. Keep them close and they grow disrespectful; keep them at a distance and they resent it.
/en/lunyu/yang-huo/25.html
子曰：唯女子与小人为难养也，近之则不孙，远之则怨。
Still disliked at forty
The Master said: One who is still disliked at forty will end that way.
/en/lunyu/yang-huo/26.html
子曰：年四十而见恶焉，其终也已。
Yin had three humane men
The Viscount of Wei left, the Viscount of Ji became a slave, and Bi Gan remonstrated and died. Confucius said: Yin had three humane men.
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/1.html
微子去之，箕子为之奴，比干谏而死。孔子曰：殷有三仁焉。
Liuxia Hui dismissed three times

Liuxia Hui served as chief judge and was dismissed three times. Someone said: Is it not time for you to leave? He said: If I serve others by the straight Way, where could I go and not be dismissed three times? If I serve others by a crooked…
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/2.html
柳下惠为士师，三黜。人曰：子未可以去乎？曰：直道而事人，焉往而不三黜？枉道而事人，何必去父母之邦？
How Duke Jing of Qi would treat Confucius

Duke Jing of Qi, discussing how to treat Confucius, said: I cannot treat him as the Ji family is treated; I will treat him somewhere between the Ji and the Meng. Then he said: I am old; I cannot make use of him. Confucius left.
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/3.html
齐景公待孔子，曰：若季氏则吾不能，以季、孟之间待之。曰：吾老矣，不能用也。孔子行。
The people of Qi send female musicians
The people of Qi sent a troupe of female musicians, and Ji Huanzi accepted them. For three days no court was held, and Confucius left.
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/4.html
齐人归女乐，季桓子受之。三日不朝，孔子行。
Jieyu, the madman of Chu

Jieyu, the madman of Chu, passed Confucius singing: Phoenix! Phoenix! How your virtue has declined! What is past cannot be corrected; what is to come can still be pursued. Give it up, give it up! Those who govern today are in peril! Confuci…
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/5.html
楚狂接舆歌而过孔子曰：凤兮！凤兮！何德之衰？往者不可谏，来者犹可追。已而，已而！今之从政者殆而！孔子下，欲与之言。趋而辟之，不得与之言。
Changju and Jieni ploughing side by side

Changju and Jieni were ploughing side by side. Confucius passed by and sent Zilu to ask them where the ford was. Changju said: Who is that holding the reins? Zilu said: It is Kong Qiu. Is it Kong Qiu of Lu? It is. Then he knows where the fo…
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/6.html
长沮、桀溺耦而耕，孔子过之，使子路问津焉。长沮曰：夫执舆者为谁？子路曰：为孔丘。曰：是鲁孔丘与？曰：是也。曰：是知津矣。问于桀溺，桀溺曰：子为谁？曰：为仲由。曰：是鲁孔丘之徒与？对曰：然。曰：滔滔者天下皆是也，而谁以易之？且而与其从辟人之士也，岂若从辟世之士哉？耰而不辍。子路行以告。夫子怃然曰：鸟兽不可与同群，吾非斯人之徒与而谁与？天下有道，丘不与易也。
Zilu meets the old man with the basket

Zilu, following the Master, fell behind and met an old man carrying a basket on his staff. Zilu asked: Have you seen my master? The old man said: Your four limbs do no work, you cannot tell the five grains apart — who is your master? He pla…
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/7.html
子路从而后，遇丈人，以杖荷蓧。子路问曰：子见夫子乎？丈人曰：四体不勤，五谷不分。孰为夫子？植其杖而芸。子路拱而立。止子路宿，杀鸡为黍而食之，见其二子焉。明日，子路行以告。子曰：隐者也。使子路反见之。至则行矣。子路曰：不仕无义。长幼之节，不可废也；君臣之义，如之何其废之？欲洁其身，而乱大伦。君子之仕也，行其义也。道之不行，已知之矣。
Men who withdrew from the world

Men who withdrew from the world: Boyi, Shuqi, Yuzhong, Yiyi, Zhu Zhang, Liuxia Hui, Shaolian. The Master said: Not lowering their aims nor disgracing themselves — that was Boyi and Shuqi. Of Liuxia Hui and Shaolian he said: They lowered the…
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/8.html
逸民：伯夷、叔齐、虞仲、夷逸、朱张、柳下惠、少连。子曰：不降其志，不辱其身，伯夷、叔齐与？谓：柳下惠、少连，降志辱身矣。言中伦，行中虑，其斯而已矣。谓：虞仲、夷逸，隐居放言。身中清，废中权。我则异于是，无可无不可。
The music masters scatter

Grand Music Master Zhi went to Qi; Gan, master of the second meal, went to Chu; Liao, master of the third meal, went to Cai; Que, master of the fourth meal, went to Qin. Fangshu the drummer went to the Yellow River region; Wu, player of the…
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/9.html
大师挚适齐，亚饭干适楚，三饭缭适蔡，四饭缺适秦。鼓方叔入于河，播鼗武入于汉，少师阳、击磬襄入于海。
The Duke of Zhou to the Duke of Lu

The Duke of Zhou said to the Duke of Lu: The gentleman does not neglect his kin. He does not give the great ministers cause to resent not being used. Old friends, unless there is a grave reason, he does not cast off. He does not expect ever…
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/10.html
周公谓鲁公曰：君子不施其亲。不使大臣怨乎不以。故旧无大故，则不弃也。无求备于一人。
Zhou had eight scholars
Zhou had eight scholars: Boda, Bokuo, Zhongtu, Zhonghu, Shuye, Shuxia, Jisui, and Jigua.
/en/lunyu/wei-zi/11.html
周有八士：伯达、伯适、仲突、仲忽、叔夜、叔夏、季随、季騧。
Seeing danger, offering his life
Zizhang said: A scholar who, seeing danger, offers his life; seeing gain, thinks of what is right; at sacrifices, thinks of reverence; in mourning, thinks of grief — such a one will do.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/1.html
子张曰：士见危致命，见得思义，祭思敬，丧思哀，其可已矣。
Holding to virtue but not broadly
Zizhang said: One who holds to virtue but not broadly, who believes in the Way but not firmly — how can it be said he has it? How can it be said he lacks it?
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/2.html
子张曰：执德不弘，信道不笃，焉能为有？焉能为亡？
Zixia and Zizhang on making friends

Zixia's disciples asked Zizhang about making friends. Zizhang said: What does Zixia say? They replied: Zixia says, 'Associate with those who are suitable; reject those who are not.' Zizhang said: That is different from what I have heard. Th…
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/3.html
子夏之门人问交于子张。子张曰：子夏云何？对曰：子夏曰：可者与之，其不可者拒之。子张曰：异乎吾所闻：君子尊贤而容众，嘉善而矜不能。我之大贤与，于人何所不容？我之不贤与，人将拒我，如之何其拒人也？
Even minor arts have something worth seeing
Zixia said: Even minor arts surely have something worth seeing; but if pursued far, one fears getting bogged down. That is why the gentleman does not pursue them.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/4.html
子夏曰：虽小道，必有可观者焉；致远恐泥，是以君子不为也。
Each day learning what he did not know
Zixia said: One who each day learns what he did not know, and each month does not forget what he has mastered, may be called fond of learning.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/5.html
子夏曰：日知其所亡，月无忘其所能，可谓好学也已矣。
Learn broadly and keep your aims firm
Zixia said: Learn broadly and keep your aims firm; ask earnestly and reflect on what is close at hand. Humaneness lies in this.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/6.html
子夏曰：博学而笃志，切问而近思，仁在其中矣。
The hundred artisans stay in their workshops
Zixia said: The hundred artisans stay in their workshops to complete their work; the gentleman learns in order to reach his Way.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/7.html
子夏曰：百工居肆以成其事，君子学以致其道。
The petty man glosses over his errors
Zixia said: When the petty man errs, he is sure to gloss it over.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/8.html
子夏曰：小人之过也必文。
The gentleman has three aspects
Zixia said: The gentleman has three aspects. From afar he looks stern; up close he is warm; when you hear him speak, he is exacting.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/9.html
子夏曰：君子有三变：望之俨然，即之也温，听其言也厉。
Win trust before working the people

Zixia said: The gentleman wins the trust of his people before he works them; without their trust, they will think he is oppressing them. He wins trust before he remonstrates; without trust, the ruler will think he is slandering him.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/10.html
子夏曰：君子信而后劳其民，未信则以为厉己也；信而后谏，未信则以为谤己也。
Great virtue does not overstep the bounds
Zixia said: In great matters of virtue, do not overstep the bounds; in small matters, some leeway is acceptable.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/11.html
子夏曰：大德不逾闲，小德出入可也。
Sprinkling and sweeping

Ziyou said: Zixia's disciples and young followers are fine when it comes to sprinkling and sweeping, answering and responding, coming forward and withdrawing. But these are mere branches; of the root they have nothing. What about that? Zixi…
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/12.html
子游曰：子夏之门人小子，当洒扫、应对、进退，则可矣。抑末也，本之则无。如之何？子夏闻之曰：噫！言游过矣！君子之道，孰先传焉？孰后倦焉？譬诸草木，区以别矣。君子之道，焉可诬也？有始有卒者，其惟圣人乎！
When one who learns has energy to spare
Zixia said: When one in office has energy to spare, he should learn; when one who learns has energy to spare, he should take office.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/13.html
子夏曰：仕而优则学，学而优则仕。
In mourning, carry grief to its fullest
Ziyou said: In mourning, carry grief to its fullest, and stop there.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/14.html
子游曰：丧致乎哀而止。
My friend Zhang does what is hard to do
Ziyou said: My friend Zhang does what is hard to do. Yet he is not yet humane.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/15.html
子游曰：吾友张也，为难能也。然而未仁。
How imposing Zhang is
Zengzi said: How imposing Zhang is! It is hard to practice humaneness alongside him.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/16.html
曾子曰：堂堂乎张也，难与并为仁矣。
People never give themselves fully, except in mourning
Zengzi said: I have heard from the Master: People never give themselves fully — except, surely, at the mourning of their parents!
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/17.html
曾子曰：吾闻诸夫子：人未有自致者也，必也亲丧乎！
The filial piety of Meng Zhuangzi

Zengzi said: I have heard from the Master: As for the filial piety of Meng Zhuangzi, the rest of it others could manage; but his not changing his father's ministers or his father's policies — that is hard to manage.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/18.html
曾子曰：吾闻诸夫子：孟庄子之孝也，其他可能也；其不改父之臣，与父之政，是难能也。
Yang Fu made chief judge

The Meng family made Yang Fu chief judge, and he asked Zengzi for advice. Zengzi said: Those above have lost the Way, and the people have long been scattered. If you get at the truth of a case, feel grief and pity, and do not rejoice.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/19.html
孟氏使阳肤为士师，问于曾子。曾子曰：上失其道，民散久矣。如得其情，则哀矜而勿喜。
Zhou's wickedness was not so extreme
Zigong said: Zhou's wickedness was not as extreme as they say. That is why the gentleman hates to dwell in low places, where all the evils of the world flow together.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/20.html
子贡曰：纣之不善，不如是之甚也。是以君子恶居下流，天下之恶皆归焉。
The faults of the gentleman are like eclipses
Zigong said: The faults of the gentleman are like eclipses of the sun and moon. When he errs, everyone sees it; when he corrects it, everyone looks up to him.
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/21.html
子贡曰：君子之过也，如日月之食焉：过也，人皆见之；更也，人皆仰之。
From whom did Zhongni learn?

Gongsun Chao of Wei asked Zigong: From whom did Zhongni learn? Zigong said: The Way of Kings Wen and Wu has not fallen to the ground; it lives among people. The worthy remember its great parts, the unworthy its small parts; there is no one…
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/22.html
卫公孙朝问于子贡曰：仲尼焉学？子贡曰：文武之道，未坠于地，在人。贤者识其大者，不贤者识其小者，莫不有文武之道焉。夫子焉不学？而亦何常师之有？
Is Zigong worthier than Zhongni?

Shusun Wushu said to the ministers at court: Zigong is worthier than Zhongni. Zifu Jingbo told Zigong. Zigong said: Compare it to the walls of a house. My wall reaches only to the shoulder, so one can peer over and see the fine rooms inside…
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/23.html
叔孙武叔语大夫于朝，曰：子贡贤于仲尼。子服景伯以告子贡。子贡曰：譬之宫墙，赐之墙也及肩，窥见室家之好。夫子之墙数仞，不得其门而入，不见宗庙之美，百官之富。得其门者或寡矣。夫子之云，不亦宜乎！
Zhongni cannot be disparaged

Shusun Wushu disparaged Zhongni. Zigong said: It is no use; Zhongni cannot be disparaged. The worthiness of other men is like hills and mounds, which can still be climbed over. Zhongni is like the sun and moon, which no one can climb over.…
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/24.html
叔孙武叔毁仲尼。子贡曰：无以为也，仲尼不可毁也。他人之贤者，丘陵也，犹可逾也；仲尼，日月也，无得而逾焉。人虽欲自绝，其何伤于日月乎？多见其不知量也！
Zhongni cannot be equalled

Chen Ziqin said to Zigong: You are just being modest. How could Zhongni be worthier than you? Zigong said: A gentleman is judged wise by one word and foolish by one word; one cannot be careless in speech. That the Master cannot be equaled i…
/en/lunyu/zi-zhang/25.html
陈子禽谓子贡曰：子为恭也，仲尼岂贤于子乎？子贡曰：君子一言以为知，一言以为不知，言不可不慎也。夫子之不可及也，犹天之不可阶而升也。夫子之得邦家者，所谓立之斯立，道之斯行，绥之斯来，动之斯和。其生也荣，其死也哀，如之何其可及也。
Yao said: Ah, you, Shun

Yao said: Ah, you, Shun! The succession ordained by Heaven rests in your person. Hold faithfully to the middle. If all within the four seas suffer hardship, Heaven's bounty will end forever. Shun likewise charged Yu with this. Tang said: I,…
/en/lunyu/yao-yue/1.html
尧曰：咨！尔舜！天之历数在尔躬。允执其中。四海困穷，天禄永终。舜亦以命禹。曰：予小子履，敢用玄牡，敢昭告于皇皇后帝：有罪不敢赦。帝臣不蔽，简在帝心。朕躬有罪，无以万方；万方有罪，罪在朕躬。周有大赉，善人是富。虽有周亲，不如仁人。百姓有过，在予一人。谨权量，审法度，修废官，四方之政行焉。兴灭国，继绝世，举逸民，天下之民归心焉。所重：民、食、丧、祭。宽则得众，信则民任焉，敏则有功，公则说。
Zizhang asks how to take part in government

Zizhang asked Confucius: What must one do to take part in government? The Master said: Honor the five excellences and banish the four evils; then you may take part in government. Zizhang said: What are the five excellences? The Master said:…
/en/lunyu/yao-yue/2.html

子张问于孔子曰：何如斯可以从政矣？子曰：尊五美，屏四恶，斯可以从政矣。子张曰：何谓五美？子曰：君子惠而不费，劳而不怨，欲而不贪，泰而不骄，威而不猛。子张曰：何谓惠而不费？子曰：因民之所利而利之，斯不亦惠而不费乎？择可劳而劳之，又谁怨？欲仁而得仁，又焉贪？君子无众寡，无小大，无敢慢，斯不亦泰而不骄乎？君子正其衣冠，尊其瞻视，俨然人望而畏之，斯不亦威而不猛乎？子张曰：何谓四恶？子曰：不教而杀，谓之虐。不戒视成，谓之暴。慢令致期，谓之贼。犹之与人也，出纳之吝；谓之有司。
Without knowing the decree of Heaven
The Master said: Without knowing the decree of Heaven, one cannot be a gentleman. Without knowing ritual, one cannot stand. Without knowing words, one cannot know people.
/en/lunyu/yao-yue/3.html
子曰：不知命，无以为君子也。不知礼，无以立也。不知言，无以知人也。

edges: 大宰问于子贡曰：夫子圣者与？
子曰：三年无改于父之道，可谓孝矣。
子夏曰：日知其所亡，月无忘其所能，可谓好学也已矣。
子曰：不患人之不己知，患其不能也。
曰：乡也，吾见于夫子而问知，子曰：举直错诸枉，能使枉者直。
南容三复白圭，孔子以其兄之子妻之。
孔子对曰：有颜回者好学，不幸短命死矣！
子曰：苟正其身矣，于从政乎何有？
子曰：博学于文，约之以礼，亦可以弗畔矣夫！
修己以安百姓，尧舜其犹病诸！
抑为之不厌，诲人不倦，则可谓云尔已矣。
多闻择其善者而从之，多见而识之，知之次也。
周之德，其可谓至德也已矣。
子曰：不在其位，不谋其政。
吾未见好德如好色者也。
子曰：不曰如之何如之何者，吾末如之何也已矣。
子曰：君子不重则不威，学则不固。主忠信。无友不如己者。过则勿惮改。
过位，色勃如也，足躩如也，其言似不足者。
入公门，鞠躬如也，如不容。
孔子曰：以吾从大夫之后，不敢不告也。
仲弓曰：雍虽不敏，请事斯语矣。
子路问曰：何如斯可谓之士矣？
子曰：苟正其身矣，于从政乎何有？不能正其身，如正人何？
子路问曰：何如斯可谓之士矣？
桓公杀公子纠，不能死，又相之。
子曰：君子欲讷于言而敏于行。
子曰：不患无位，患所以立；不患莫己知，求为可知也。
宰予昼寝。子曰：朽木不可雕也，粪土之墙不可杇也，于予与何诛。子曰：始吾于人也…
孔子曰：益者三乐，损者三乐。
孔子曰：君子有三畏：畏天命，畏大人，畏圣人之言。
孔子曰：君子有三戒：少之时，血气未定，戒之在色；及其壮也，血气方刚，戒之在斗…
孺悲欲见孔子，孔子辞以疾。
子路曰：昔者由也闻诸夫子曰：亲于其身为不善者，君子不入也。
宽则得众，信则民任焉，敏则有功，公则说。
曾子曰：吾闻诸夫子：孟庄子之孝也，其他可能也；其不改父之臣，与父之政，是难能也。
陈司败问：昭公知礼乎？孔子曰：知礼。孔子退，揖巫马期而进之，曰：吾闻君子不党…
Fan Chi asked. Answer: The humane put the hard work first and the reward after.
Yan Yuan asked. Answer: To overcome the self and return to ritual is humaneness.
Zhonggong asked. Answer: What you do not want for yourself, do not impose on others.
Sima Niu asked. Answer: The humane are slow to speak.
Fan Chi asked. Answer: Love people.
Fan Chi asked. Answer: Be respectful at home, reverent in your duties, and loyal to others.
Zigong asked. Answer: Serve the worthiest of its high officers; befriend the most humane of its scholars.
Zizhang asked. Answer: Respectfulness, generosity, trustworthiness, diligence, kindness.
Meng Yizi asked. Answer: Do not go against it.
Meng Wubo asked. Answer: Let your parents' only worry be that you might fall ill.
Ziyou asked. Answer: Without reverence, what is the difference?
Zixia asked. Answer: The countenance is the hard part.
Zigong asked. Answer: Enough food, enough arms, and the trust of the people.
Duke Jing of Qi asked. Answer: Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son.
Zizhang asked. Answer: Keep it in mind without weariness; carry it out with loyalty.
Ji Kangzi asked. Answer: To govern is to set right.
Ji Kangzi asked. Answer: You govern; what need is there for killing?
Zilu asked. Answer: Go before them; toil for them.
Zhonggong asked. Answer: Put your officers to work first, pardon small faults, promote the worthy and able.
the Duke of She asked. Answer: Those near are pleased, and those far away come.
Zixia asked. Answer: Do not seek speed; do not look to small gains.
Zizhang asked. Answer: Honor the five excellences; banish the four evils.
Zigong asked. Answer: He acts first, and his words follow.
Sima Niu asked. Answer: The gentleman is free from anxiety and fear.
Zilu asked. Answer: He cultivates himself with reverence.
Zizhang asked. Answer: Plain and upright and loving what is right, attentive to words and observant of faces, mindful to put himself below others.
Zigong asked. Answer: He conducts himself with a sense of shame, and when sent on missions abroad he does not disgrace his ruler's commission.
Zilu asked. Answer: Earnest, encouraging, and genial.
Fan Chi asked. Answer: Devote yourself to what is right for the people; revere the spirits but keep them at a distance.
Fan Chi asked. Answer: Know people.
Zizhang asked. Answer: Hold to loyalty and trustworthiness, and move toward what is right.
Fan Chi asked. Answer: Put the work first and the reward after.
Good to use: Name a child Hongyi, or just Hong or Yi. Hong is a wide heart, yi a tough spirit; together they are this line's meaning. Good for boys or girls.

Good to use: One line, four names: Zhidao, Jude, Yiren, Youyi. Siblings can take one each, and in order they make the sentence. Yi here means the six arts (ritual, music, archery, charioteering, writing, numbers), so Youyi is not about idle play.
Good to use: Names: Delin, Youlin, Bugu. Someone of virtue will always find people drawing near. Also a good name for a small shop or a community reading room.
Good to use: Names: Duzhi, Jinsi, Qiewen, Boxue. Jinsi means thinking from what is close at hand, not shallow thinking.
Good to use: Use song (pine) or bai (cypress) in a name; a study or shop can be called Houdiao or Suihan. The point: only in the cold do you see who does not wither, who can stand hardship.
Good to use: Names: Leshan, Leshui, Renjing. Le here means to delight in (read lè). The mountain stands for steadiness, water for flow; two children could take one each.
Good to use: Names: Minxing, Shenyan, Minzhi. Quick to act, careful in speech: for families who hope their child will be steady.
Avoid: Do not use qiaoyan (clever words) in a name: the line says such people are rarely humane.
Avoid: Do not use kengkeng in a name: it describes a narrow, rigid mind.
Avoid: Do not use xiangyuan in a name: Confucius calls the village worthy a thief of virtue.
Good to use: The first line of the Analects, the most natural choice for the start of school. For a child, add: learn it, then go and practise; once you can do it, you will be glad.
Use with care: Xi means practising again and again, not just reviewing the textbook.
Good to use: The best line for a teacher's first lesson: if you do not understand, raise your hand. Saying so is no shame; pretending to understand is what costs you.
Good to use: For a child starting a new class or choosing a major: knowing it is not as good as liking it; liking it is not as good as finding joy in learning it.
Good to use: For new classmates and roommates: everyone around you has something to learn from; when you see someone's fault, check whether you have it too.
Use with care: The second half says to correct what is not good in yourself; it is not only about finding good teachers.
Good to use: For older students preparing for exams: study as if you cannot catch up, and once you have, fear losing it.
Good to use: Can be made into a term plan: learn one new thing each day, and each month look back to see you have not forgotten. Wang here means wu, 'without'.
Good to use: For teachers and parents: help a child only when they are eager to work it out, or trying to say it and cannot. At the start of term, do not hand over every answer.
Good to use: Confucius starts from age fifteen. At a coming-of-age ceremony you can say: set your aim at fifteen, stand on your own at thirty, and the years between are yours.
Use with care: Li at thirty means standing firm with a mind of one's own, not only starting a family and a career.

Good to use: Being an adult means governing yourself. Yikonglu reads keji as restraining oneself: you manage your own conduct without waiting for others to. The following words, 'humaneness comes from oneself', say the same.
Good to use: For a child becoming independent: when things go wrong, first ask what you failed to do, then look at others.
Good to use: Pifu means an ordinary person, man or woman. The commander of a great army can be captured, but no one can take away an ordinary person's resolve.
Good to use: For a first job search or choosing a major: do not worry about having no position; worry about what qualifies you to stand in it.
Good to use: As an adult no one covers your mistakes. This line is five characters: when you err, do not fear to correct it.

Good to use: A graduation speech can give the original meaning: when your work is done well and you have strength left, keep learning; when your learning is solid and you have strength left, go and serve. Learning and doing alternate all your life.
Use with care: You means having strength to spare, not 'excellent grades'. Reading it as 'study well and you should become an official' gets it backwards.
Good to use: Best for a teacher seeing graduates off: how do we know your future will not surpass our present?
Use with care: The second half says that someone who has made no name by forty or fifty is not to be held in awe: it urges the young to work while they can, not only praises them.
Good to use: For those just entering working life: do not worry that no one knows you; go and know others, understand others.

Good to use: For students heading to work or graduate school. The rest of the line: serve the worthiest of the officials, befriend the most humane of the scholars. The best tools are good mentors and good friends.
Use with care: Originally Zigong asked how to practise humaneness, and Confucius used the craftsman as a comparison; it is not only about tools.
Good to use: Ideal for a class yearbook or graduation photo: friends gathered through study, and through friends we become better.
Good to use: A closing line for a graduation speech. Before it: a scholar must be broad and resolute, for the road is long and the load heavy.

Good to use: Zizhang asked how to seek office, and the answer is how to do a job: listen widely and set aside what you are unsure of, speak carefully even of what you are sure of; look widely and hold back from what you doubt. Few errors in speech, few regrets in action: there lies your living.
Good to use: Do the work in hand well first, then talk about pay. It does not say never discuss money; pay follows what you have done. Once the work is done, you can name your price with confidence.
Good to use: Three questions before leaving work: was I wholehearted in what I did for others? Did I keep my word to colleagues? Have I practised what I learned?
Good to use: For someone taking over a new project: rushing for results means none come; eyeing small gains means big things are not achieved.
Good to use: A workplace code in nine characters: be respectful at rest, earnest at work, wholehearted with people. Confucius says never drop these wherever you go.
Good to use: A newcomer should not decide things above their role; look after your own part.
Use with care: Often used to shirk: 'not my business'. The line already appears at 8.14, where Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: if those in office ask you, you must still tell them truthfully.

Good to use: Usable, but know its weight: Confucius ranks 'a sense of shame in conduct' and 'not disgracing the ruler's commission' first, and 'words must be trusted, deeds must be carried through' only third, calling such people kengkeng, which Zhu Xi reads as narrow.
Use with care: Keeping your word is the floor, not the highest praise; whether to do something depends on whether it is right, not on having said it.

Good to use: Yikonglu follows a Qing reading: this line is about husband and wife, valuing the other's virtue above looks. What follows covers serving parents, serving a ruler and friendship: four lines, four human bonds. A wedding officiant can start from here.

Good to use: Confucius chose a son-in-law by character alone. Gongye Chang was in prison at the time; Confucius said it was not his crime and gave him his daughter anyway. Told at a wedding by the bride's parents, it means: we chose you for who you are.
Good to use: Nan Rong kept reciting the ode about words that cannot be taken back, so Confucius gave him his niece in marriage. For the couple: in daily life, be careful in speech.
Good to use: For newlyweds: two people need not agree on everything; they can differ and still be in harmony. Going along with everything while resenting it inside is what disharmony really is.

Good to use: Harmony in the home is most precious. But the second half says harmony without measure will not work either. At a wedding, 'harmony is most precious' can be followed by 'talk things through, and keep to rules'.
Use with care: Often taken as 'smooth everything over'; the text in fact warns against seeking harmony at any cost.

Good to use: Guanju is the first ode of the Book of Songs, about a gentleman seeking a good wife. Confucius says it is joyful without excess, sorrowful without harm. If Guanju is read at a wedding, this line can follow.
Good to use: Confucius' wish: to give the old ease, friends trust, and the young care. At a one-month celebration, elders can say: now the family has one more little one to care for.
Good to use: A blessing for a newborn: who knows that this child will not surpass us as we are today?
Good to use: Confucius taught his son Kong Li only two things: study the Odes, or you will not know how to speak; study ritual, or you will not know how to stand. A family motto for a first birthday.
Use with care: Chen Kang suspected Confucius taught his son extra in private; he had not. He taught his son just as he taught his students, another point worth sharing with new parents.

Good to use: Can be written as a family motto: be filial at home, respectful outside, careful in action, true in speech, generous to all, close to the humane. It goes on: with strength to spare, study letters. Read books, but character comes first.
Good to use: Only at three does a child leave its parents' arms. New parents up at night with a baby will read this and know they were carried the same way.
Use with care: This comes from Confucius' dispute with Zai Wo over three years of mourning; its point is parents' kindness. On a card the line alone is fine, but leave out the mourning context.

Good to use: On New Year's Day, looking at the river. Zhu Xi reads it as heaven and earth never pausing, urging us never to pause in learning; most people today read it as time flowing away like water. Both fit the New Year: one is to cherish, the other is to keep going.
Good to use: For a year-end review: were you wholehearted for others? true to your friends? have you practised what you learned? Once a year is not enough; Zengzi asked himself daily.

Good to use: Write New Year plans under this line: a mound one basket short, and it is you who stopped; a single basket on level ground, and it is you who went forward. Success or not, it is up to you.
Good to use: For turning the page: last year's errors, once corrected, are gone; left uncorrected, they become true errors.
Good to use: The best line for going home for the New Year: remember your parents are a year older, glad of their long life and anxious that they are ageing.
Good to use: Write it on the new year's plan: without thought for what is far, trouble is close at hand.
Good to use: The safest line for a birthday of an elder: the humane live long. Before it: the wise delight in water, the humane in mountains, so a birthday couplet can start from mountains and water.

Good to use: By age: at fifty 'knowing the decree of heaven', at sixty 'an ear attuned', at seventy 'following the heart's desire without overstepping'. Confucius said these of himself; from the young to the old they are praise, not assessment.
Good to use: For elders still studying and busy: so absorbed he forgets to eat, so happy he forgets his worries, not noticing old age coming. Confucius said this was the kind of man he was.
Good to use: A rule for the birthday banquet: when villagers drank together, Confucius left only after the elders with staffs had gone. Young people should not leave the table first.
Good to use: Suited to the elder's own speech: in old age, remind yourself not to be grasping. It does not suit the young lecturing their elders with it.
Avoid: Never use this at a birthday.

Use with care: Here Confucius scolds one old acquaintance, Yuan Rang, who sat squatting waiting for him: not deferential as a youth, nothing to show as an adult, then he tapped his shin with his staff. The three lines go together and target this man, not all old people.
Good to use: When his student Boniu fell ill, Confucius visited and held his hand through the window. What matters most in visiting the sick is to go and to hold their hand.
Use with care: Confucius goes on to say 'we are losing him, it is fate', grief at knowing Boniu would die. Do not repeat this when visiting the sick.
Good to use: Illness is one of the three things Confucius was most careful about. For the patient's family: do not let illness drag on; follow the doctor's advice.
Good to use: When visiting a sick child or urging children to take care: parents can let go of everything except worry over their child's illness. Taking care of yourself is filial piety.
Good to use: Gravely ill, Confucius said he would rather die among his students than at the hands of retainers. The people at the bedside matter more than ceremony.

Good to use: When Confucius was ill and the ruler visited, he could not rise, so he laid his court robe over himself to receive him. The sick keep their dignity too, and visitors should leave them their dignity.
Avoid: Do not say this to someone who is ill.

Use with care: Zixia said this to console Sima Niu, who feared for his brothers; it is followed by 'the gentleman is reverent without fault, respectful and courteous to others'. Fate is not in our hands; what we can do is govern ourselves. Said alone to a patient, it sounds like telling them to give up.
Good to use: Most used in eulogies and funeral couplets: honour the departed with care, remember the distant ancestors, and people's hearts grow generous.
Good to use: Better true grief than a perfect funeral. A simple ceremony is fine so long as the heart is there.
Good to use: When Yan Yuan died, Confucius wept so hard his followers tried to calm him; he said: if not for this man, for whom should I grieve? For mourning a dearest friend.
Good to use: Confucius' first words on hearing of Yan Yuan's death: Heaven is destroying me. For losing a student or a companion on the way.
Use with care: Zhu Xi says Confucius grieved that the Way had no one to carry it on, not that he himself would die.
Good to use: Etiquette on the day of condolence: eating beside the bereaved, Confucius never ate his fill; on a day he had wept, he did not sing.
Good to use: When a friend died with no family to see to him, Confucius said: I will take care of the funeral. The weightiest words between friends.
Good to use: To comfort the bereaved: express your grief fully, but do not harm your health.
Use with care: Zhu Xi says the words 'and stop there' are a little brief, and may lead people to skip the details of ritual.
Good to use: The full statement on filial piety: in life, serve them by ritual; in death, bury them and sacrifice to them by ritual. For mourning parents.
Good to use: For a child going far away, always with the second half: if you go, let your parents know where. Today that means texting when you arrive and telling them when you move.
Use with care: Often only the first half is quoted, to stop someone leaving. Zhu Xi's point is not to leave your parents unable to find you, not that you may not go.
Good to use: Best for someone going abroad to work or study: treat people with respect and courtesy, and wherever you go there will be people like brothers.

Use with care: These are Zixia's words to console Sima Niu; first comes 'the gentleman is reverent without fault, respectful and courteous to others'. Only on that condition are all within the four seas brothers.
Good to use: For someone changing jobs or cities: what is past cannot be changed; what is to come can still be reached.

Use with care: This was sung to Confucius by the Chu recluse Jieyu, urging him to stop pursuing office; when Confucius wanted to speak to him, he hurried away. Fine to use in farewell, but do not present it as Confucius' words.
Good to use: When a friend takes a road you disagree with: advise sincerely, speak kindly; if they will not listen, stop, and do not let advice ruin the friendship.
Good to use: When parting, plan the next meeting: when you come back from afar, we will gather again.
Good to use: For when the fundamental paths differ and you cannot work together.
Use with care: Often used to part ways over small differences. Zhu Xi means the difference between good and evil, right and wrong; differences in method or opinion do not count.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says the Way cannot be put into words. Confucius likewise says Heaven never speaks, yet the four seasons still run their course.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Achieving without dwelling on it” (功成而弗居): Shun and Yu possessed the world but did not treat it as their own.
Cited by commentators: Lü Huiqing, explaining “Do not display what is desirable, so the people's hearts are not disturbed,” cites Confucius's answer to Ji Kangzi: if you yourself were not covetous…

Cited by commentators: Heshang Gong cites this line to explain “not exalting the worthy,” writing 远美人 (“keep beautiful people at a distance”) for 远佞人 (“keep flatterers at a distance”). One character makes the difference.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Confucius calls for “promoting the worthy and able,” and Laozi says “do not exalt the worthy.” On employing people, the two schools are exact opposites.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi speaks of “softening the glare and mingling with the dust” (和其光，同其尘), and Confucius of “harmonious but not the same” (和而不同). Both speak of harmony, but one merges with others while the other keeps itself.

Cited by commentators: Du Daojian notes that Laozi often says “what the ancients called” or “the established sayings have it.” He is retelling the ancients, just like Confucius's “I transmit and do not create.”

Read alongside by Yikonglu: “He puts himself last, and finds himself first” (后其身而身先): think of others first and you end up standing firm yourself. Confucius too says “wishing to stand, he helps others stand.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says “the highest good is like water,” and Confucius says “the wise delight in water.” Confucians and Daoists both compare people to water.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Looking at the same water, Confucius saw time that never stops.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Rich and noble yet arrogant, one brings blame on oneself” (富贵而骄，自遗其咎). Confucius also says “rich without arrogance” is not enough: one should be “rich and love ritual.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Better to stop than to fill it to the brim” (持而盈之，不如其已) is about knowing when to stop. Confucius gives warnings for three stages: youth, prime, and old age.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Clear and reaching in all four directions, can you be without knowing?” (明白四达，能无知乎). Confucius too says he is “without knowledge,” and when someone asks him, he probes the question from both ends.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Heshang Gong reads “the gate of Heaven” (天门) as the north pole. Confucius compares governing by virtue to the Pole Star.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says a vessel is useful because of its “emptiness” (无). Confucius says the gentleman must not be a mere vessel.
Cited by commentators: Wu Cheng cites Dong Sijing: Confucius's “four do-nots” begin with looking, which matches Laozi's “the five colors blind the eye” and “for the belly, not for the eye.”
Cited by commentators: Wang Pang, explaining “I have great trouble because I have a body,” cites Confucius's “no ego” (毋我) and says the principle is the same.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Favor and disgrace alike are alarming” (宠辱若惊): before getting something you fear not getting it, and once you have it you fear losing it. This is just Confucius's “base fellow” (鄙夫).
Cited by commentators: “Valuing one's own person as one values the world” (贵以身为天下): commentators adapt Confucius's praise of Shun and Yu, who “possessed the world yet did not take it as their own.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Hold to the Way of old to manage what exists now” (执古之道，以御今之有): Confucius too says he is “faithful to antiquity and loves it.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Only by knowing the principles of old can you handle what is in front of you. Confucius calls it “reviewing the old to understand the new” (温故而知新).
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Hesitant, as if crossing a river in winter” (豫兮若冬涉川): as careful as someone crossing an icy river in winter, just like Zengzi when he quoted the Songs.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Solemn, like a guest” (俨兮其若客): grave and dignified like a guest. Confucius says that when you go out, act as if you were meeting an honored guest.

Cited by commentators: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, explaining “not knowing the constant, one acts rashly, and misfortune follows” (不知常，妄作，凶), cites this line: a person without constancy will meet with disgrace.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says that with the best ruler, the people merely know he exists. Confucius too praises Shun for “governing without acting” (无为而治).
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “When trust is lacking, there is distrust” (信不足焉，有不信焉): Confucius too puts trust ahead of food and arms.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The ruler stays still and everyone naturally turns around him. This is exactly what Laozi calls “the very highest” (太上).

Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says filial piety and kindness only show up when the six relations are out of harmony. Confucius says that when those above are filial and kind, those below will be loyal. The same words, read two ways.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Confucians make filial piety the root of humaneness, but Laozi says “When the great Way is abandoned, there are humaneness and righteousness.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi wants to “abandon cleverness and discard profit,” and Confucius likewise detests “clever words and an ingratiating face.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Between 唯 and 阿, how great is the difference?” (唯之与阿，相去几何): 唯 is the respectful reply of a disciple to his teacher, and it is the word Zengzi used to answer Confucius.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “What others fear, one cannot fail to fear” (人之所畏，不可不畏): Confucius speaks of three things the gentleman holds in awe.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says “cut off learning and you will have no worries” (绝学无忧). Confucius says a whole day spent thinking is not as good as learning.

Cited by commentators: Chunfu's commentary, recorded by Jiao Hong, cites Su Shi's “what passes is like this, yet it has never gone,” using Confucius's sigh by the river to explain “from ancient times to now…”

Read alongside by Yikonglu: Heshang Gong reads “return it whole” (全而归之) as returning one's body intact to one's parents. This is exactly what Zengzi did on his deathbed: “Uncover my feet, uncover my hands.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him” (夫唯不争，故天下莫能与之争). Confucius too says the gentleman has nothing to contend over.

Cited by commentators: Su Zhe, explaining “one who is at one with loss, loss too is glad to have” (同于失者，失亦乐得之), cites Confucius: one who sets his heart on humaneness will do no evil, and how much more one who sets it on the Way.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says a whirlwind does not last the whole morning, while Confucius likens the gentleman's virtue to the wind. The same word, wind, used two ways.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “One who boasts has no merit” (自伐者无功): Yan Yuan's wish was precisely never to boast of his own good qualities.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Meng Zhifan guarded the rear in a retreat, and on entering the city said his horse would not go faster, refusing to take credit.

Cited by commentators: Jiao Hong records Li Yue's reading 法地地，法天天，法道道 and cites as evidence the pattern of Confucius's 君君臣臣父父子子 (“let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son”).
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says “Heaven is great, Earth is great, and the king too is great.” Confucius praises Yao: “Only Heaven is great, and only Yao modeled himself on it.”

Read alongside by Yikonglu: The excavated texts read “the gentleman travels all day without leaving his baggage wagons” (君子终日行不离其辎重). Confucius says “a gentleman without gravity has no dignity” (君子不重则不威).
Cited by commentators: Su Zhe, explaining “good speech leaves no flaw to fault,” speaks of “speaking only when the time is right,” a phrase that comes from this chapter.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: “The good person is the teacher of the one who is not good; the one who is not good is the material of the good person.” Confucius says that both the good and the bad can be our teachers.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Always good at saving people, so no one is cast aside” (常善救人，故无弃人): Confucius too says teaching makes no distinction of background.

Cited by commentators: Jiao Hong records Lü Huiqing citing “How lofty were Shun and Yu, possessing the world yet not taking it as their own!” to explain “The world is a sacred vessel; it cannot be acted upon.”
Cited by commentators: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang's commentary uses “the succession ordained by Heaven rests on your person” (历数在躬), from Yao's words when handing the throne to Shun.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Achieve the result without pride, achieve it without boasting” (果而勿矜，果而勿伐). The commander Confucius wanted was likewise one who “approaches a task with caution and succeeds through careful planning.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says “do not use arms to dominate the world,” and Confucius says the people must be taught for seven years before they go to war. Neither takes up arms lightly.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Weapons are instruments of ill omen” (兵者不祥之器): war is one of the three things Confucius treated with the greatest care.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Duke Ling of Wei asked about battle formations. Confucius said he had never studied them, and left the next day.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Once regulation begins there are names; once there are names, one should know when to stop” (始制有名，名亦既有，夫亦将知止). Confucius wants names rectified, and Laozi says that once names are established, one must know when to stop.

Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains “one who conquers himself is strong” as “able to overcome the self and restore one's nature” (克己复性), clearly adapting Confucius's “overcome the self and return to ritual” (克己复礼).
Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains “The great Way floods everywhere; it can go left or right” with Confucius's words about himself: “nothing I must do, nothing I must not do” (无可无不可).
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Achievement accomplished without claiming the name" (功成不名有): Confucius praises Yao, and the people could not say what was good about him.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The Dao, when spoken, is bland and tasteless" (道之出口，淡乎其无味): pleasant words do not hold people for long.

Cited by commentators: Emperor Xuanzong of Tang defends "What is to be shrunk must first be stretched" (将欲歙之，必固张之) by citing Confucius: "One may stand firm with someone, yet not be able to weigh circumstances with him." This, he says, is expedience…

Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says "The Dao constantly does nothing, yet nothing is left undone" (道常无为而无不为). Confucius likewise says Shun "simply made himself reverent and faced south, nothing more."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The excavated manuscripts read "Heaven and earth will right themselves" (天地将自正). Confucius says, "If you lead with rectitude, who will dare not be upright?"
Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains "Superior virtue is not virtuous" (上德不德) by citing Confucius at seventy: "I followed what my heart desired without overstepping the bounds."
Cited by commentators: Emperor Xuanzong explains "Ritual is the thinning of loyalty and trust" (礼者忠信之薄) by citing Confucius: is ritual merely jade and silk?
Cited by commentators: Jiao Hong records Xizhai's commentary, which uses Confucius's "My Way has one thread running through it" to explain "Those of old who attained the One" (昔之得一者).
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Reversal is the movement of the Dao" (反者道之动): Confucius too knew that, beyond holding to the constant, one must adapt to change.
Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains "When the superior scholar hears the Dao, he practices it diligently" (上士闻道，勤而行之) and says Yan Hui was just such a superior scholar.

Cited by commentators: Jiao Hong records Lü Huiqing's commentary. Lü cites "Hear the Way in the morning, and one may die in the evening content" and says the superior scholar is one who has truly understood the Dao.
Cited by commentators: Wang Pang explains "The great vessel is completed late" (大器晚成) by citing Confucius's remark that Guan Zhong was a small vessel.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The violent and strong do not die a natural death" (强梁者不得其死): Confucius had the same worry about the hard and unbending Zilu.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Teaching without words" (不言之教) is teaching by example. Confucius says that if you yourself are upright, things get done without orders.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Teaching without words" (不言之教): Confucius too says Heaven does not speak, yet the four seasons run their course.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi asks "Fame or your person, which is dearer?" (名与身孰亲). Confucius, by contrast, dreads dying without a good name. Here Confucians and Daoists clash head-on over "name."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Great eloquence seems tongue-tied" (大辩若讷): Confucius too says those slow of speech are close to ren.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Great fullness seems empty" (大盈若冲): Master Zeng says his friend (Yan Yuan, per Zhu Xi) had yet seemed to have nothing, and was full yet seemed empty.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "No calamity is greater than not knowing contentment" (祸莫大于不知足): Confucius says a state should fear unequal distribution more than scarcity.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Laozi says "Without going out the door, one knows the world" (不出户，知天下). Confucius says thinking without learning is of no use.

Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains "In pursuing learning, one gains daily" (为学日益) by citing Confucius's "hear much, choose the good and follow it," and calls this only "the next level of knowing."

Cited by commentators: Su Zhe goes on to cite Confucius asking Zigong: "I am not one who learns much and remembers it. I have one thread running through it all." This, Su says, is exactly "in pursuing the Dao, one loses daily" (为道日损).
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Those who are not good, I also treat with goodness" (不善者吾亦善之). Confucius instead advocates "repay resentment with uprightness."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: This chapter of Laozi is entirely about life and death. Confucius says: not yet understanding life, how can one understand death?
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Produces but does not possess, acts but does not presume" (生而不有，为而不恃): possessing the world without treating it as one's own.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Block the openings, shut the doors" (塞其兑，闭其门): Laozi shuts the gates of eyes and ears, while Confucius teaches not to look at or listen to what is contrary to ritual.
Cited by commentators: Wang Bi explains "having wealth and goods in excess" (财货有余) with Confucius's words "if not obtained by the proper way."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The people love byways" (民好径), while Confucius's school praised Tantai Mieming for "never taking shortcuts": the same little path.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Cultivate it in the person, and its virtue will be genuine" (修之于身，其德乃真), extending step by step to the whole world. Confucius says "cultivate oneself to bring peace to the people."
Cited by commentators: Heshang Gong explains "Those who speak do not know" (言者不知) with Zigong's saying "a team of four horses cannot overtake the tongue."

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Those who know do not speak; those who speak do not know" (知者不言，言者不知). Confucius says the virtuous will surely have something to say, but those who have something to say are not necessarily virtuous.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Heshang Gong says "value deeds, not words" (贵行不贵言). Confucius says the gentleman is slow in speech and quick in action.

Cited by commentators: Jiao Hong records Xizhai's commentary, which cites "when the wind passes over the grass, it must bend" to explain "I do nothing, and the people transform of themselves" (我无为而民自化).
Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains "The more laws and orders are displayed" (法令滋彰) by citing Confucius's passage on rectifying names: "the people will not know where to put hand or foot."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "I do nothing, and the people transform of themselves" (我无为而民自化). Confucius too praises Shun for "governing by non-action."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Straight but not overbearing" (直而不肆): straightness needs measure. Confucius says straightness without ritual wounds others.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Sharp-edged but not cutting" (廉而不刿): Confucius was "gentle yet stern, awe-inspiring yet not fierce." It is the same "A yet not B" pattern.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "For governing people and serving Heaven, nothing is better than frugality" (治人事天莫若啬): Confucius's governance also stresses "economy in expenditure and love for the people."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Governing a great state is like cooking a small fish" (治大国若烹小鲜): commentators explain it through Shun's non-action, and Confucius praises Shun in the same way.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "When the Dao oversees the world, ghosts lose their spirit-power" (以道莅天下，其鬼不神). Confucius says to respect ghosts and spirits but keep them at a distance.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "A great state is like the lower reaches of a river" (大国者下流): Zigong says the gentleman most dreads dwelling in the low place, yet Laozi wants the great state to accept the low place willingly.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "If a great state lowers itself to a small state, it wins the small state" (大国以下小国，则取小国). Confucius says that if distant people do not submit, one should cultivate civil virtue to draw them in.

Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains "Why abandon those who are not good?" (人之不善，何弃之有) with "one who does wrong in the morning yet hears the great Dao in the evening," adapting Confucius's "hear the Way in the morning."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Why abandon those who are not good?" (人之不善，何弃之有): Confucius too says that in teaching he made no distinction of background.
Source: In the Analects, someone puts "repay resentment with virtue" (报怨以德) to Confucius, who answers "repay resentment with uprightness." Zhu Xi notes: "What this person cites…"

Cited by commentators: Lü Huiqing explains "Light promises surely lack trust" (轻诺必寡信) through "words that can be made good" (复言). The phrase comes from Master You: "When trust is close to righteousness, one's word can be made good."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "A nine-story terrace rises from a heap of earth" (九层之台，起于累土): Confucius says that if you stop when the mound is one basketful short, it is you who stopped.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Not to enlighten the people but to keep them simple" (非以明民，将以愚之): the two lines are often compared, and both depend on how the old commentaries read them.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: Wang Bi says that if you govern a state by cleverness, the people respond with cleverness. Confucius says that if you govern the people by punishments, they will avoid them but have no sense of shame.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "To be ahead of the people, one must put oneself behind them" (欲先民，必以身后之): Confucius says that in governing, you yourself should lead the way and take on the toil first.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him" (以其不争，故天下莫能与之争).
Cited by commentators: Jiao Hong records Wang Pang's commentary, which uses Confucius's "In ritual, frugality is better than extravagance" to explain "the second is frugality" (二曰俭).
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Compassionate, hence able to be brave" (慈故能勇): Confucius too says the humane are surely brave.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Frugal, hence able to be generous" (俭故能广). Confucius says "economy in expenditure and love for the people."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The good warrior is not martial" (善为士者不武): war was among the matters Confucius treated with the greatest caution.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "No calamity is greater than underestimating the enemy" (祸莫大于轻敌): what Confucius wanted was someone who "approaches affairs with fear."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Military strategists have a saying" (用兵有言), yet Confucius said he had never studied military matters.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Wearing coarse cloth while holding jade in the bosom" (被褐怀玉): it is the same jade, but Confucius would "sell it!" while Laozi keeps it tucked away.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Those who understand me are few" (知我者希). Confucius too sighed, "No one understands me!"
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Those who understand me are few; those who follow me are rare" (知我者希，则我者贵). Confucius says not to resent it when others do not understand you.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "To know that one does not know is highest" (知不知，上): the line where the two schools come closest.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Confucius calls himself ignorant, which fits neatly with Laozi's "knowing that one does not know."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "When the people do not fear authority, a greater terror arrives" (民不畏威，则大威至). Confucius speaks of the three things the gentleman holds in awe.
Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains "The way of Heaven does not contend yet excels at winning, does not speak yet excels at responding" by citing Confucius's "What does Heaven ever say?"
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Bravery in daring means death" (勇于敢则杀): this is exactly what Confucius feared for Zilu.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Bravery in not daring means life" (勇于不敢则活): Confucius wanted nothing to do with someone who would fight a tiger bare-handed or wade across a river.
Cited by commentators: Su Zhe explains "The people do not fear death" (民不畏死), again citing Confucius: "the people will not know where to put hand or foot."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "There is always the executioner who does the killing" (常有司杀者杀). Confucius asks why governing should need killing at all.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Confucius says that if good people governed a state for a hundred years, they could overcome cruelty and do away with killing.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The people starve because their rulers tax them too heavily" (民之饥，以其上食税之多). Master You urges Duke Ai to lower taxes: "If the people have enough, with whom will the ruler lack?"
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The people are hard to govern because those above meddle" (民之难治，以其上之有为). Confucius says that if those above are upright, those below will not dare to be otherwise.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The strong and great stay below, the soft and weak stay above" (强大处下，柔弱处上): Master Zeng says his friend (Yan Yuan, per Zhu Xi) had yet seemed to have nothing, and was full yet seemed empty.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The way of Heaven reduces surplus and makes up deficiency" (天之道，损有余而补不足). Confucius says the worry is not scarcity but inequality.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Who can take his surplus to serve the world?" (孰能有余以奉天下): Confucius says the gentleman helps those in urgent need and does not add to the wealth of the rich.

Cited by commentators: Lü Huiqing explains "One who takes on the state's disgrace is called lord of the altars" (受国之垢，是谓社稷主) by citing Tang's words: "If the myriad regions have sinned, the sin rests on my own person"…
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Taking on the state's misfortunes" (受国不祥): blame yourself much and others little.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Reconcile a great resentment, and some resentment surely remains" (和大怨，必有余怨). Confucius advocates "repay resentment with uprightness, and virtue with virtue."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The virtuous hold the tally; the virtueless hold the che" (有德司契，无德司彻): che was the Zhou tax system, and Master You urged Duke Ai to adopt it.
Cited by commentators: Jiao Hong records Wang Pang's commentary: the Analects and the Mencius both close by invoking Yao, Shun, Yu and Tang, and Laozi ends with this chapter for the same purpose.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Neighboring states within sight of one another… the people reach old age and death without ever visiting each other." Confucius, by contrast, wants those near to be glad and those afar to come.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Trustworthy words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not trustworthy" (信言不美，美言不信). Confucius says: "Clever words and an ingratiating face: seldom is there ren in them."
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "The good do not argue" (善者不辩). Confucius says the gentleman is slow in speech and quick in action.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: "Those who know are not broadly learned; the broadly learned do not know" (知者不博，博者不知). Confucius teaches broad learning restrained by ritual.
Source: The two lines “By nature people are close; by practice they grow far apart” (性相近，习相远) come straight from Confucius's own words.
Cited by commentators: Mencius's mother moved house three times to find the right neighbors. Commentators all explain the story with this chapter: choose a place to live where humaneness prevails.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “What will one do when old?” (老何为): if one does not study when young and has made no progress by forty or fifty, one is not worth being in awe of.
Cited by commentators: The Beiyao commentary closes its exhortation to study with Yang Huo's words urging Confucius to take office: time does not wait for us.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Jade uncut does not become a vessel” (玉不琢，不成器): Zigong uses the Songs to say a person must be shaped the way jade is worked, by cutting, filing, carving and polishing.

Read alongside by Yikonglu: Artisans complete their work in their workshops, and the gentleman reaches the Way through learning. This follows directly on “If people do not learn, they do not know what is right” (人不学，不知义).
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Keep close to teachers and friends” (亲师友): which friends? Three kinds: the upright, the trustworthy, and the well-informed.
Cited by commentators: “Filial and fraternal duty first, knowledge second” (首孝悌，次见闻): Wang Xiang and Atsumi both cite this chapter to support that order.
Cited by commentators: How to use “knowledge” (见闻): listen much, look much, and set aside whatever you are unsure of.
Cited by commentators: Kong Rong giving up the pears teaches a younger brother's duty. Youzi says filial and fraternal duty is the root of humaneness.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The Three Bonds set out the roles of ruler and minister, father and son, husband and wife. In Confucius's version, each first fulfills his own part.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “These four seasons revolve without end” (此四时，运不穷): Heaven does not speak, yet the seasons still run their course.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “In accord with the center” (应乎中): the Pole Star stays in the center without moving, and all the stars turn around it.
Cited by commentators: The Yinshu commentary explains the “Five Constants” with Huang Kan's subcommentary on this chapter: the Three Bonds and Five Constants do not change for a hundred generations.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Trustworthiness (信) is the last of the Five Constants: if a person cannot be trusted, I do not know what he can do.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The passage on the six grains goes well with this line from the old man with the basket: one whose limbs do not toil cannot even tell the five grains apart.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: However important the six domestic animals are, they count for less than people. When the stable burned, Confucius asked only whether anyone was hurt.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The seven emotions need not be extinguished, only kept in measure: joy without excess, grief that does no harm.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The eight sounds are musical instruments. Confucius speaks of what music is for: a person's character is finally completed in music.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Music is more than bells and drums. Read this alongside the “eight sounds” (八音).

Read alongside by Yikonglu: “The ruler respectful, the minister loyal” (君则敬，臣则忠): the ruler treats his ministers with ritual, and the minister serves his ruler with loyalty. Each side has its own duty.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The spirit of the Ten Duties: each role fulfills its own part.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “When the Elementary Learning is done, go on to the Four Books” (小学终，至四书): first learn how to be a person, then study texts with the energy left over.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Begin with sweeping, answering and replying, and rise step by step. That is the path from the Elementary Learning to the Four Books.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The first chapter shows what “recording good words” (记善言) looks like: one saying, one principle.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Confucius had already called the two characters in the title Zhongyong (中庸, the Mean) the highest virtue.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Read the passage on the three Changes alongside Confucius saying he would study the Changes in his later years.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: This one line of Confucius covers the order of the Songs, Rites and Music among the Six Classics.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Our Duke of Zhou made the Rites of Zhou” (我周公，作周礼): Confucius says the Zhou rites drew on the Xia and Shang, so he follows Zhou.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Rites and music complete” (礼乐备): Confucius told his son that without learning ritual he would have nothing to stand on.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The “transmit” (述) in “transmitting the sages' words” (述圣言) is the same 述 as in Confucius's “I transmit and do not create.”
Cited by commentators: On why one “should recite and chant” (当讽咏) the Songs, the Beiyao commentary cites this very chapter.
Cited by commentators: Wang Xiang explains Yao with this very line in which Confucius praises Yao.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Tang and You Yu” (唐有虞) refers to Yao and Shun. Shun governed the world with five worthy ministers.
Cited by commentators: King Wu of Zhou's “ten ministers of 乱”: here 乱 means to govern, so these are ten ministers able to set disorder right.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The Three Kings of Xia, Shang and Zhou followed one another, and their rites were added to and cut back in ways that can be known.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: What it looks like when “the royal order fell” (王纲坠): rites, music and military campaigns no longer come from the Son of Heaven.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “The Five Hegemons grew strong” (五霸强): Confucius both praises and criticizes two of the hegemons.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The hegemons had their merits too: Confucius credits Guan Zhong with setting the whole world in order.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The word “usurped” (篡) in “Wang Mang usurped” (王莽篡) is the label historians fixed on him. Once the name is settled, right and wrong are clear.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Before he usurped the throne, Wang Mang was humble and courteous. Judge people over a long time, not by a single moment.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Historians argued over which of the Three Kingdoms was legitimate, and what they were arguing about was names and roles.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The Sui “passed the throne on no further and lost the line” (不再传，失统绪). Confucius had said long before that a realm gained by improper means lasts only a few generations.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The text says “received the abdication of Zhou” (受周禅), while commentators write “usurped” (篡): the dispute is between name and reality.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Most rulers of the Five Dynasties were generals who seized the throne, and their dynasties often fell within one or two reigns.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: The Liao and Jin rulers who proclaimed themselves emperors can be read against this line of Confucius: whether a state truly has a ruler depends on whether it has ritual.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Powerful eunuchs ran rampant” (权阉肆): Confucius says governing requires keeping glib flatterers at a distance.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Disaster often starts close at hand. The Ming fell to its eunuchs, trouble from right “within the screen wall.”
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Recite with the mouth, ponder with the mind” (口而诵，心而惟): reciting is learning and pondering is thinking. Neither can be left out.
Cited by commentators: “At it in the morning, at it in the evening” (朝于斯，夕于斯): Wang Xiang says this is practicing it constantly.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “It records order and chaos, so one knows rise and fall” (载治乱，知兴衰): reading history lets you infer later ages, and Confucius says a hundred generations can be known.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Confucius took Xiang Tuo as his teacher. He had no fixed teacher and learned from whoever had the Way.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Already in office, he studied all the harder” (彼既仕，学且勤): whatever energy is left over from office should still go to study.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Tying one's hair to a beam and jabbing one's thigh with an awl are stories of hard study. Confucius said that when he was learning, he forgot to eat.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Grinding away is not the same as knowing how to learn: learning without thinking still leaves you confused.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: On the “lofty” (卓) in “still toiling for the lofty” (犹苦卓): Yan Yuan says Confucius's learning stands lofty before him, and however hard he follows he cannot reach it.
Cited by commentators: Su Xun “first resolved to strive” (始发愤) at twenty-seven, and the Yinshu commentary cites this line of Confucius to explain 发愤.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Confucius set his heart on learning at fifteen, while Su Xun only resolved to strive at twenty-seven. Read the two side by side.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Child prodigies were ones “people called marvels” (人称奇). Confucius says the young deserve awe, but he also warns that anyone still unknown at forty or fifty does not.
Cited by commentators: After the child prodigies, the Beiyao commentary closes with “learning what is below and reaching what is above”: beyond cleverness, one must learn step by step.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “One should take warning oneself” (当自警): the warning is for yourself, not something to use against others.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Cai Wenji and Xie Daoyun were able to learn, and teaching has never made distinctions of background.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Liu Yan held office at seven, while Confucius only set his heart on learning at fifteen. Early or late does not matter. What matters is resolve.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: Liu Yan's answer about the character 朋 mocked factions. Read it with Confucius's “sociable but not partisan.”
Cited by commentators: “A person who does not learn is worse than a creature” (人不学，不如物): the expanded commentary (增注) uses this line of Confucius.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Learn when young, act when grown” (幼而学，壮而行): learning and doing take turns for a whole lifetime.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Make your name known” (扬名声): the gentleman fears reaching the end of his life with nothing worth praising.
Cited by commentators: On the “benefit” (益) in “play brings no benefit” (戏无益), the Yinshu commentary cites this chapter: real progress takes slow work and cannot be rushed.
Read alongside by Yikonglu: “Play brings no benefit” does not mean no play at all. Confucius too says “take your ease in the arts.”
Source: Book of Songs, Wei Feng, Qi Yu: “As if cut, as if filed; as if carved, as if polished.” (如切如磋，如琢如磨。)
Source: Book of Songs, Lu Song, Jiong: “Thoughts without swerving; so the horses go forth.” (思無邪，思馬斯徂。)
Source: Book of Songs, Wei Feng, Shuo Ren: “Her artful smile so lovely, her fine eyes so clear.” (巧笑倩兮，美目盼兮。)
Source: Book of Songs, Xiao Ya, Xiao Min: “In fear and trembling, as if at the edge of a deep abyss, as if treading on thin ice.” (戰戰兢兢，如臨深淵，如履薄冰。)
Source: Book of Songs, Bei Feng, Xiong Zhi: “Neither envious nor grasping: how could he not be good?” (不忮不求，何用不臧。)
Source: Book of Songs, Xiao Ya, Wo Xing Qi Ye: “Truly it is not for wealth, but only for novelty.” (成不以富，亦祇以異。)
Source: Book of Songs, Bei Feng, Pao You Ku Ye: “Where it is deep, wade through in your clothes; where it is shallow, lift your hem.” (深則厲，淺則揭。)
Source: Mencius, Teng Wen Gong I, chapter 2: Zengzi said, “In life, serve them according to ritual; in death, bury them according to ritual and sacrifice to them according to ritual…”
Source: Mencius, Gongsun Chou I, chapter 7: Confucius said, “Humaneness is what makes a neighborhood beautiful.” (孔子曰：里仁為美。)
Source: Mencius, Gongsun Chou I, chapter 7: “If one chooses not to dwell in humaneness, how can one be wise?” (擇不處仁，焉得智？)
